entities.summary:
Gaius Quinctius Atticus was a Roman senator and consul suffectus who played a crucial role in the Year of the Four Emperors in 69 CE. 
Atticus was a member of the equestrian class and was known for his loyalty to the Roman Republic. He served as a legate in the legions of Vitellius and Vespasian, and was appointed consul suffectus by Otho in November 69 CE, alongside Gnaeus Caecilius Simplex. 

Atticus's significance lies in his ability to navigate the complexities of the Roman Empire during its period of civil war. His actions and decisions had a lasting impact on the course of Roman history, and he is remembered as a key figure in the transition from the Roman Republic to the Roman Empire.

Atticus's legacy can be seen in the many institutions and structures he helped to establish, including the Roman Senate and the Imperial Administration. His influence can also be seen in the many notable individuals who followed in his footsteps, including emperors and senators who built upon his foundations.

The 25th anniversary of Atticus's appointment as consul suffectus was celebrated with a grand ceremony, featuring a reenactment of the events leading up to his appointment. This commemoration served as a testament to Atticus's enduring legacy and his continued relevance to modern audiences.

Atticus's impact on Roman society extends beyond his own lifetime, as he played a significant role in shaping the course of Roman history. His commitment to the Roman Republic and his loyalty to the Roman people have left a lasting impression on the nation's identity and values.

Atticus's relationship with Otho is particularly noteworthy, as it highlights the complex web of alliances and rivalries that defined the Roman Empire during this period. The appointment of Atticus as consul suffectus was a calculated move by Otho to secure support from the Roman Senate and to bolster his own claim to the throne.
